title: Ecclesiastical traditions fall under Isaiah — later pastors' human precepts
source_text: XXIX. Praeterea valde notandum est quod in sua responsione adversarii concedunt, nempe Christum ibi reprehendere traditiones quasdam a quibusdam Mose & Prophetis recentioribus acceptas. Etenim inde sequitur pari saltem jure damnandas, & rejiciendas esse traditiones illas quas Pontificii Ecclesiasticas vocant, id est, multa quibus putatur Deus coli, & quae tamen nec Christus, nec Apostoli ejus instituerunt, sed Pastores & Doctores posteriorum saeculorum: quae certe traditiones magnam partem constituunt institutorum Ecclesiae Romanae. Nam traditiones illae non sunt minus mandata & praecepta hominum quam quae olim a senioribus Judaeorum instituta erant. Ideoque non minus in illas congruunt Isaiae verba a Christo prolata, atque confirmata, Frustra colunt me docentes doctrinas & mandata hominum.
pass_a_gloss: Besides, it is very much to be noted that in their reply the adversaries concede that Christ there rebukes certain traditions received from some more recent than Moses and the Prophets. For from this it follows that at least by equal right those traditions which the Pontiffs call Ecclesiastical are to be condemned and rejected — that is, many things by which God is thought to be worshipped, and which nevertheless neither Christ nor His Apostles instituted, but pastors and doctors of later ages: which traditions certainly make up a great part of the Roman Church's institutes. For those traditions are no less commandments and precepts of men than those which were once instituted by the Jewish elders. And so Isaiah's words, brought forward and confirmed by Christ, fit them no less: In vain they worship Me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men.
pass_b_english: Note Rome's own concession: Christ rebuked traditions from teachers later than Moses and the Prophets.

By the same right, so-called Ecclesiastical traditions fall — rites and worship practices invented by later pastors and doctors, not by Christ or the Apostles — and those make up much of Rome's system.
They are no less human commandments than the Jewish elders' once were.
Isaiah's words, cited and confirmed by Christ, fit them equally: In vain they worship Me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men (Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:9; Mark 7:7).

choices.why: Le Blanc's third tradition-kind from XIV-XV.
Concession boomerangs onto Rome's own customs.
